title: Burning chest pain after meals in general practice
desc: This station involves a focused chest pain history and examination of a 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and asthma who has had four months of daily burning retrosternal pain after meals. The candidate then interprets his ECG and blood tests, gives a diagnosis and differentials, and outlines GP management of reflux (lifestyle changes, a PPI trial and when to refer for endoscopy) without missing a cardiac cause, then safety-nets.
focus: Chest pain history: telling reflux from cardiac pain, GORD management and when to refer for endoscopy
stem: You are a GP registrar in a suburban general practice. Carl Gleeson, a 54-year-old administrative worker at a warehouse, has booked an appointment because of chest pain. He is comfortable and pain-free in the waiting room. A practice nurse is available, and the practice has a 12-lead ECG machine.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Gleeson and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you the results of investigations. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Carl Gleeson, a 54-year-old administrative worker at a warehouse. You are friendly and relaxed, a bit fed up with the pain, and you have no pain right now. You are sitting in a chair. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I've been getting this burning pain in my chest for a few months now, and it's starting to get to me."

History (give only when asked):

  • Onset and timing: it started about 4 months ago. It comes on about once a day, usually after dinner, and each episode lasts about half an hour. Sometimes it comes after lunch at work as well.
  • Site: in the centre of your chest, behind the breastbone (point to it). It does not spread anywhere: not to the arm, jaw, neck or back.
  • Character and severity: burning. About 5 out of 10.
  • What makes it better: "Not that I have noticed." You have not tried any medicines for it.
  • What makes it worse: lying down, eating (it is worse after meals, especially big ones) and exercise. "It's definitely worse after a spicy meal, like my curries or chilli." If asked more about exercise: "It's worse if I walk to the shops straight after dinner. It doesn't seem to come on by itself when I'm playing tennis, and stopping doesn't make it go away; it lasts half an hour either way." You love spicy food and have a curry or chilli dish most nights.
  • Reflux symptoms (only if asked): yes, you often get a sour, acid taste at the back of your throat, mostly when you lie down at night. You have had a dry cough for a few months, worse at night; you thought it was your asthma, but your breathing is otherwise fine. The burning sometimes wakes you at night. You eat dinner at about 8 pm and go to bed at about 9.30 pm. You sometimes feel a bit of indigestion in the upper tummy after a big meal.
  • Alarm features (all no): no trouble swallowing food or drink, no pain on swallowing, no food sticking. No weight loss (your weight has been steady), no vomiting, no vomiting blood, no black or tarry stools, no unusual tiredness.
  • Heart (all no): no sweating, nausea, breathlessness or sense of doom with the pain. No pain that comes on with exertion and settles with rest. No palpitations, fainting or dizziness. No breathlessness lying flat, no waking breathless, no ankle swelling. No recent viral illness. No tearing pain going through to the back.
  • Lungs (all no): no sharp pain on breathing in, no breathlessness, no coughing up blood, no calf pain or swelling, no recent travel or surgery, no recent chest infection.
  • Other (all no): no pain in the right upper tummy or shoulder blade, no yellow skin or eyes, no pale or greasy stools, no dark urine. No injury to the chest, no bruising. No rash. You do not feel anxious or panicky.
  • Past history: asthma since you were 5, well controlled; you use your puffer only every few weeks. Type 2 diabetes diagnosed 12 years ago, "moderately controlled", according to your GP. No heart problems, no stomach ulcers, no operations.
  • Medicines: salbutamol puffer when needed, metformin twice a day. No over-the-counter medicines (no anti-inflammatories such as ibuprofen, no aspirin), no vitamins or supplements, no recreational drugs.
  • Allergies: penicillin (you get a rash). Vaccinations are up to date.
  • Family history: your mother has type 2 diabetes, diagnosed at 42. Your father is healthy. Your brother has had asthma since childhood, well controlled. No family history of heart attacks, stomach or oesophageal cancer, or Barrett's oesophagus that you know of. You have no children.
  • Social: you have never smoked. You drink about 4 standard drinks a week. A couple of coffees a day at work. You play tennis for 2 hours every weekend and walk to the shops, which are 10 minutes away. You eat home-cooked meals and like spicy food. You live with your partner in an apartment in the suburbs and have plenty of friends and family around.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you are not sure what is causing it. Your main concern: "It's making concentrating on my work so hard, especially after my lunch breaks!" You would like something to fix it.

Use plain language and say you do not follow if the candidate uses jargon. Give a realistic answer if asked something outside the script.

If the candidate asks for an ECG in Part 1: the nurse says, "I'll record it now," and the examiner hands it over in Part 2.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General inspection: comfortable, well-looking man, overweight with central weight. No pallor, jaundice, cachexia or distress.
  • Vital signs: heart rate 76 beats/min, regular. Blood pressure 134/82 mmHg (right arm); 132/80 mmHg left arm if asked. Respiratory rate 14 breaths/min. SpO2 98% on room air. Temperature 36.7°C. Capillary blood glucose 8.4 mmol/L (2 hours after lunch).
  • Measurements: weight 92 kg, height 178 cm, BMI 29.0 kg/m², waist 104 cm.
  • Hands, face and neck: no clubbing, no conjunctival pallor, no xanthelasma. No cervical or supraclavicular lymph nodes, including the left supraclavicular fossa. JVP not raised.
  • Cardiovascular: pulse regular, normal character. Apex beat not displaced. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs (no ejection systolic murmur), no rub. No peripheral oedema. Peripheral pulses present.
  • Chest wall and skin: no tenderness on palpation of the chest wall or ribs, no bruising, no rash.
  • Respiratory: normal expansion, resonant, vesicular breath sounds, no wheeze or crackles.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender, including the epigastrium and the right upper quadrant. Murphy's sign negative. No masses, no hepatomegaly or splenomegaly.
  • Calves: soft, non-tender, no swelling.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduces self (name and role), confirms Carl's identity, gains consent and mentions confidentiality.
Uses open questions and plain language, acknowledges the effect of the pain on his work, and summarises back to Carl.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Onset and timing: began 4 months ago, about once a day after dinner, each episode lasting about half an hour.
Site and radiation: central, retrosternal, with no radiation.
Character and severity: burning, 5 out of 10.
Aggravating and relieving factors: worse lying down, after meals, with spicy food and with exercise after eating; nothing relieves it.

check.x: Asks about reflux symptoms: acid or sour taste in the throat (present), a chronic dry cough (present, worse at night) and being woken at night by symptoms.
Asks about alarm features: difficulty or pain swallowing, weight loss, vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools, and tiredness or symptoms of anaemia (all absent).

Clarifies the link with exercise and screens for cardiac ischaemia: whether pain comes on with exertion alone and eases with rest, and whether there is sweating, nausea, breathlessness or a sense of doom with it.
Asks cluster questions for at least 5 other causes from more than 2 systems:

kids.x: Other gastrointestinal: indigestion or upper abdominal pain (peptic ulcer); right upper quadrant pain to the shoulder blade, jaundice, pale stools, dark urine (biliary colic); food sticking with chest pain (oesophageal spasm).

Other cardiovascular: orthopnoea, PND, ankle swelling (heart failure); fainting or breathlessness on exertion (aortic stenosis); recent viral illness (pericarditis); tearing pain to the back (dissection).
Respiratory: pleuritic pain, breathlessness, haemoptysis, calf swelling, recent travel or surgery (PE); sudden pleuritic pain (pneumothorax); recent illness (pleurisy).
Other: chest trauma or bruising (rib fracture), dermatomal rash (shingles), palpitations, sweating and panic (anxiety).

check.x: Takes the past history: asthma since age 5 (well controlled) and type 2 diabetes for 12 years (moderate control).

Takes a medication history: salbutamol and metformin; specifically asks about over-the-counter NSAIDs or aspirin, supplements and recreational drugs; penicillin allergy (rash); vaccinations up to date.
Takes a family history: mother with type 2 diabetes, father healthy, brother with asthma; asks specifically about oesophageal or gastric cancer, Barrett's oesophagus and premature heart disease.
Takes a social history: never smoked, about 4 standard drinks a week, caffeine, a spicy diet with a late dinner close to bedtime, exercise (tennis, walking), work and home supports.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: unsure of the cause, worried about concentrating at work after lunch, wants it fixed.
Examination
Asks for vital signs (HR, BP, RR, SpO2, temperature) and capillary glucose, and measures weight, BMI and waist (BMI 29.0, waist 104 cm: central obesity).
General inspection for pallor, jaundice and cachexia, and checks the lymph nodes, including the left supraclavicular fossa.
Examines the cardiovascular system: pulse, JVP, heart sounds and murmurs (including aortic stenosis), and peripheral oedema.
Examines the respiratory system: breath sounds, wheeze and crackles.
Examines the abdomen: epigastric and right upper quadrant tenderness (Murphy's sign), masses and hepatomegaly.
Palpates the chest wall for tenderness, looks for a rash or bruising, and checks the calves.
Requests a 12-lead ECG because the pain is worse with exercise in a 54-year-old man with diabetes.
Interpretation
Reads the ECG systematically: sinus rhythm at 74, normal axis and intervals, no ST or T wave changes, no Q waves or LVH, unchanged from the ECG 3 years ago.
States that a normal resting ECG does not exclude stable angina, so the exercise link still has to be clarified in a 54-year-old man with diabetes.
Interprets the full blood count and LFTs: Hb 148 g/L with a normal MCV and ferritin (no anaemia or iron deficiency to suggest bleeding) and normal LFTs (against a biliary or liver cause).

Interprets the diabetes results: HbA1c 7.6% (60 mmol/mol), above the usual target of 7% or less (53 mmol/mol), with a raised fasting glucose of 8.1 mmol/L, which adds to his cardiovascular risk; lipids are within the laboratory ranges, and eGFR and urine ACR are normal.
Gives GORD as the most likely diagnosis and justifies it: burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down and with spicy food, acid taste and a night cough, with a normal ECG and bloods.
Names peptic ulcer disease and Barrett's oesophagus or oesophageal adenocarcinoma as differentials, and stable angina as the cause not to miss, each with a feature for or against.
Management
Gives at least 3 tailored lifestyle measures (smaller or less spicy and fatty meals, earlier dinner 2 to 3 hours before bed, raise the head of the bed, weight loss).
Starts a standard-dose PPI once daily (e.g. esomeprazole 20 mg, omeprazole 20 mg, pantoprazole 40 mg) for 4 to 8 weeks with review.

Addresses endoscopy correctly: not urgent because there are no alarm features; refers for routine gastroscopy because of new-onset symptoms at over 50, OR (if quoting a 55 threshold) plans gastroscopy if symptoms do not respond to the PPI trial, recur on step-down, or alarm features develop.

Plans cardiac and diabetes follow-up: calculates his cardiovascular risk, arranges stress testing or cardiology review if the pain comes on with exertion alone or does not respond to the PPI, and plans a diabetes review for the HbA1c.
Safety netting

Gives at least 3 reflux red flags in plain words (food sticking or trouble swallowing, weight loss, repeated vomiting, vomiting blood, black stools, feeling pale and tired), with ED for vomiting blood or black stools, calling 000 if vomiting a lot of blood or feeling faint or collapsing, and prompt GP review for the others.

Gives cardiac red flags in plain words: call 000 for chest pain that is different from his usual burning (heavy or tight, spreading to the arm, jaw or back, or with sweating, breathlessness or light-headedness) and is severe, getting worse or lasts more than 10 minutes; see the GP the same or next day if chest pain starts to come on with exertion and settle with rest.

Arranges review in 4 to 8 weeks for PPI response and step-down, and follows up the gastroscopy result (or refers for gastroscopy if the PPI trial fails, symptoms recur on step-down or alarm features develop).
Answers Carl's question honestly: the tests are reassuring but do not completely exclude the heart, and explains which warning signs to act on.

part2.lead: Here is Carl's 12-lead ECG, recorded today by the practice nurse, and the blood tests from his diabetes review two weeks ago.
part2.patient:
Before question 4, the examiner reads Carl's question aloud:

  • "So it's not my heart, then?"

He is relieved, and happy with the plan if it is explained clearly.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (today)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, resting, recorded today by the practice nurse. Carl was pain-free at the time. Standard calibration (10 mm/mV, 25 mm/s).

  • Rate: 74 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus, regular.
  • Axis: +30°.
  • PR interval: 160 ms.
  • QRS: 90 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QT: 370 ms, QTc 410 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments and T waves: isoelectric ST segments in all leads; no ST elevation or depression; upright T waves in I, II, aVF and V2 to V6; no T wave inversion.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves. No left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria.
  • Comparison: ECG from 3 years ago (diabetes review): sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, normal. No change.
  • Conclusion: normal sinus rhythm; normal ECG, unchanged from 3 years ago.
handover.model:
Read: sinus rhythm at 74, normal axis, normal PR, QRS and QTc, no ST or T wave changes, no Q waves, no LVH. Unchanged from 3 years ago.

For Carl: a normal resting ECG, recorded pain-free. It shows no previous infarction and no ischaemia at rest, which fits a non-cardiac cause. It does not exclude stable angina: the resting ECG is often normal between episodes. He is a 54-year-old man with diabetes whose pain is worse with exercise, so the history matters. His pain is burning, lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does, is not relieved by rest, and does not come on with tennis on its own.

What it changes: no urgent cardiac pathway. Treat as reflux, but calculate his cardiovascular risk. Arrange functional testing or cardiology review if the pain comes on with exertion alone or does not respond to a PPI trial.

handover.label: Blood tests (diabetes review, 2 weeks ago, fasting)
handover.model:
Read: Hb 148 g/L with a normal MCV and ferritin. Normal white cells and platelets. Normal electrolytes, creatinine and eGFR (above 90). Normal bilirubin, ALP, GGT, ALT and albumin. Fasting glucose 8.1 mmol/L and HbA1c 7.6% (60 mmol/mol), up from 7.4%. Lipids are within the laboratory ranges, and the urine albumin to creatinine ratio is normal.

For Carl: no anaemia or iron deficiency, so no laboratory sign of chronic blood loss from oesophagitis, an ulcer or a cancer. Normal LFTs make a biliary or liver cause less likely. His diabetes is above the usual HbA1c target of 7% or less (53 mmol/mol), which adds to his cardiovascular risk and is one reason the cardiac differential is kept open. No kidney involvement.

What it changes: no alarm finding, so gastroscopy is not urgent, though a routine one is still indicated for new-onset symptoms over 50. Plan a diabetes review and enter these lipids into a cardiovascular risk calculation.

ask: You are now calling your GP supervisor. Please give an ISBAR handover of Carl Gleeson, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Carl now, here in general practice, including whether he needs an endoscopy.
Carl asks: "So it's not my heart, then?" Please answer him, then tell me what else you would tell him before he goes home and what follow-up you would arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, GP registrar. Patient is Carl Gleeson, 54.
  • Situation: 4 months of daily burning retrosternal pain after meals; pain-free now. Worse lying down, with spicy food and with exercise after eating. Acid taste, night cough, no alarm features.
  • Background: T2DM for 12 years on metformin, asthma, penicillin allergy (rash), never smoked.
  • Assessment: normal examination, BMI 29, waist 104 cm. ECG: sinus 74, normal intervals, no ST/T changes, unchanged; reassuring, but does not exclude stable angina. Hb 148, normal ferritin (no anaemia), normal LFTs. HbA1c 7.6%, above target. Likely GORD.
  • Recommendation: lifestyle changes, a PPI trial for 4 to 8 weeks, routine gastroscopy referral (new-onset symptoms over 50; not urgent, no alarm features), CVD risk calculation and cardiac testing if pain persists or is exertional, diabetes review.

Most likely: gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. Burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down and with spicy food, an acid taste and a night cough. Normal ECG and bloods.

  • Peptic ulcer disease: for: post-prandial indigestion. Against: no epigastric tenderness, no NSAIDs, no anaemia.
  • Barrett's oesophagus or oesophageal adenocarcinoma: for: male, over 50, night reflux, central obesity (risk factors that matter if reflux becomes chronic). Against: no dysphagia, weight loss or anaemia; only a 4-month history. Only gastroscopy and biopsy can exclude it.
  • Stable angina (must not miss): for: 54, male, diabetes, worse with exercise. Against: burning, lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does and not relieved by rest, not brought on by tennis, worse lying down, acid taste, normal ECG.
  • Biliary colic: against: no RUQ pain, normal LFTs, Murphy's negative.

1. Explain likely reflux; ECG and bloods reassuring.
  2. Lifestyle: smaller meals; less spicy and fatty food, alcohol and coffee. No food for 2 to 3 hours before bed or exercise (earlier dinner). Raise the head of the bed. Lose weight.
  3. PPI trial: standard dose once daily 30 to 60 minutes before a meal (e.g. esomeprazole 20 mg) for 4 to 8 weeks: diagnostic and therapeutic. Antacid with alginate as needed for breakthrough. Famotidine is an alternative. Then step down to the lowest effective dose.
  4. Gastroscopy: not urgent, as no alarm features. Routine referral now for new-onset symptoms over 50; or, if using a 55 threshold, refer if no response to the PPI trial, symptoms recur on step-down, or alarm features develop.
  5. CVD risk calculation; stress testing or cardiology if exertional or no response. Diabetes review.

• Call 000 for chest pain that is different from his usual burning (heavy or tight, spreading to the arm, jaw or back, or with sweating, breathlessness or light-headedness) and is severe, getting worse or lasts more than 10 minutes. GP the same or next day if chest pain starts to come on with exertion and settle with rest.
  • Reflux red flags (at least 3): food sticking or trouble swallowing, weight loss, repeated vomiting, feeling pale and tired: see the GP promptly. Vomiting blood or black stools: go to ED; call 000 if vomiting a lot of blood or feeling faint or collapsing.
  • Follow-up: review in 4 to 8 weeks for the PPI response and step-down. Gastroscopy referral and a review of the result (or referral if the PPI fails).
  • "So it's not my heart?" The tests are reassuring but do not completely exclude it, so act on the warning signs above.

ddx.for: Four months of daily burning retrosternal pain after dinner, worse lying down and with spicy food, with an acid taste in the throat, a night cough and a normal ECG and bloods.
ddx.against: Nothing relieves it yet, though he has not tried any treatment.

ddx.for: Post-prandial pain with some upper abdominal indigestion after big meals.
ddx.against: No epigastric tenderness, no NSAID or aspirin use, and a normal haemoglobin and ferritin.

ddx.for: Male, over 50, with nocturnal reflux and central obesity (waist 104 cm): risk factors that matter if his reflux becomes chronic.
ddx.against: No dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting or anaemia, and a short 4-month history.

ddx.for: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes above target, whose pain is worse with exercise.
ddx.against: Burning pain that lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does and is not relieved by rest, is not brought on by tennis, is worse lying down with an acid taste, and a normal ECG.

ddx.for: Pain after meals in an overweight man.
ddx.against: Pain is central and retrosternal, not right upper quadrant, with no jaundice, normal LFTs and a negative Murphy's sign.

guide:
In Part 1, give findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate asks for an ECG, say the nurse will record it and it will be handed over in Part 2; credit item 22 for the request. A history of about 6 minutes followed by a brief focused examination is expected. Item 9 follows the source's marking: credit it when the candidate asks cluster questions for at least 5 differentials from more than 2 systems. In Part 2, hand over both results together and ask all four questions in order. Carl's questions are credited against the management and safety-netting items wherever they are answered. For item 33, credit either a routine referral now (over 50) or a clear plan to refer if the PPI fails or alarm features arise (55 threshold).

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain fully and pins down the exercise link (worse when walking after dinner, not brought on by tennis, not relieved by rest). They screen for alarm features and for cardiac, respiratory and biliary causes, and ask for an ECG. In Part 2 they read the ECG systematically and say that a normal resting ECG does not exclude angina. They name GORD with peptic ulcer and Barrett's or adenocarcinoma, and give tailored lifestyle advice and a PPI trial with dose, timing and duration. They refer for routine gastroscopy because Carl has new-onset symptoms over 50 (or give a clear plan to refer if the PPI fails), and keep a cardiac plan open given his diabetes.

A borderline candidate diagnoses reflux without asking about exertion or ordering an ECG, treats a normal ECG as excluding angina, omits alarm-feature questions, gives a PPI without a duration or review, or does not know when endoscopy is indicated. Labelling the pain cardiac and sending Carl to ED is not wrong for safety, but it misreads the history.
explain:
The diagnosis: gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

Carl has four months of daily burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down and after spicy food. He also has an acid taste in his throat at night and a chronic dry cough, which are atypical reflux symptoms often mistaken for asthma. His examination, ECG and bloods are normal. GORD is mainly a clinical diagnosis. GORD is reflux of stomach contents that causes troublesome symptoms or complications (Montreal definition); mild symptoms on 2 or more days a week, or moderate to severe symptoms on 1 or more days a week, are usually troublesome. Carl's are daily. Risk factors include obesity (raised intra-abdominal pressure), diet (high-fat meals, citrus, tomato products, spicy food, fizzy drinks), alcohol and caffeine, asthma, a sliding hiatus hernia (common, especially with erosive or severe reflux), pregnancy and motility disorders (scleroderma, achalasia). Carl's late dinner, curries, central obesity and asthma all fit.

Not missing the heart

Chest pain worse with exercise in a 54-year-old man with diabetes must make you consider stable angina. Diabetes also makes atypical ischaemic symptoms more common. The history separates the two:

  • Angina: brought on by exertion and settles within minutes of rest.
  • Carl's pain: comes after meals, is made worse by walking soon after eating, lasts about 30 minutes whatever he does, and does not come on with tennis on its own.

Angina can also be worse after a heavy meal, so the post-prandial link alone does not exclude it; the duration and the lack of response to rest are what discriminate.

A resting ECG is the right first test. A normal one recorded pain-free does not exclude coronary disease. If the pain comes on with exertion alone, or does not respond to a PPI trial, arrange functional testing or cardiology review. Calculate his absolute cardiovascular risk with the Australian CVD Risk Calculator, and improve his diabetes control (HbA1c 7.6% against a usual target of 7% or less).

Differentials

  • Peptic ulcer disease: dyspepsia, epigastric pain, NSAID use, Helicobacter pylori. If dyspepsia is the main problem, test for H. pylori, either by urea breath test (PPIs stopped for 2 weeks and antibiotics for 4 weeks beforehand) or by biopsy at gastroscopy.
  • Barrett's oesophagus and oesophageal adenocarcinoma: see below. Dysphagia, weight loss, fatigue or anaemia suggest cancer.
  • Biliary colic: right upper quadrant pain to the scapula after fatty meals; jaundice, pale stools and dark urine with obstruction.
  • Oesophageal spasm: chest pain that can mimic myocardial infarction, often with dysphagia.
  • Other causes in the cluster screen: PE, pneumothorax and pleurisy (pleuritic pain, breathlessness); heart failure, aortic stenosis, pericarditis and dissection; rib fracture, shingles and anxiety.

Interpreting the results

The ECG is normal and unchanged from 3 years ago. The FBC and ferritin show no anaemia or iron deficiency, so there is no sign of chronic blood loss. Normal LFTs argue against a biliary or liver cause. The raised HbA1c and fasting glucose are a separate problem that adds to his cardiovascular risk.

Managing GORD (eTG)

  • Lifestyle first:
    • Smaller meals.
    • Cut down on high-fat meals, alcohol, coffee, chocolate, citrus, tomato products, spicy food and fizzy drinks.
    • Drink between meals rather than with them.
    • Avoid eating or drinking for 2 to 3 hours before bed or vigorous exercise.
    • Raise the head of the bed for night-time symptoms.
    • Lose weight; stop smoking (not relevant for Carl).
  • Drug treatment, stepwise:
    • For mild or intermittent symptoms: an antacid with alginate, or a magnesium hydroxide with aluminium hydroxide preparation, as needed.
    • If that is not enough: an H2 receptor antagonist (famotidine; ranitidine is no longer available in Australia).
    • For frequent or more severe symptoms like Carl's: a proton pump inhibitor once daily, 30 to 60 minutes before a meal, for 4 to 8 weeks (for example esomeprazole 20 mg, omeprazole 20 mg or pantoprazole 40 mg). The trial is both diagnostic and therapeutic.
    • Then step down to the lowest effective dose or on-demand use, and review regularly.
  • Surgery: laparoscopic fundoplication wraps the gastric fundus around the lower oesophagus to make a cuff. It is kept for troublesome volume reflux or a large hiatus hernia that medical treatment does not control.

When to do an endoscopy

  • Alarm symptoms: dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, anaemia, haematemesis or melaena (urgent).
  • No response to a PPI trial.
  • New-onset symptoms in an older patient (sources give over 50 or over 55). Carl is 54 with new-onset symptoms over 50, so a routine gastroscopy is reasonable now. If the 55 threshold is used, a PPI trial with gastroscopy if it fails, if symptoms recur on step-down or if alarm features develop is also acceptable.
  • Uncertain diagnosis.
  • Surveillance of known Barrett's oesophagus, with biopsy to look for dysplasia.

Barrett's oesophagus (source teaching)

Barrett's oesophagus is a complication of chronic reflux. The normal squamous lining of the lower oesophagus is replaced by columnar epithelium with intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells). This is an adaptation to acid exposure. It can progress to dysplasia and then oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

  • Risk factors: at least 5 to 10 years of GORD, age over 50, male sex, white race, hiatus hernia, central obesity, nocturnal reflux, current or past smoking, and a first-degree relative with Barrett's or adenocarcinoma.
  • At endoscopy: salmon-coloured tongues of mucosa extend up from the gastro-oesophageal junction into the pale pink squamous mucosa.
  • Explaining it to a patient (source Option 2): first check what they understand. Then explain, in small chunks and without jargon:
    • The cells at the bottom of the gullet have changed to a type of cell that copes better with acid.
    • This is not cancer, but it carries a higher risk of turning into cancer.
    • It is watched with regular camera tests (a tube passed down the throat) to look at and sample the cells.
    • Any abnormal areas can be removed.
    • Monitoring is lifelong.
  • Management: ongoing acid suppression and endoscopic surveillance. The interval depends on the findings, including whether there is dysplasia.

Other complications of GORD

  • Oesophagitis with chronic bleeding and anaemia.
  • Peptic stricture causing dysphagia.
  • Barrett's oesophagus.

Safety netting and follow-up

  • Call 000 for chest pain that is different from his usual burning (heavy, tight or crushing, spreading to the arm, jaw, neck or back, or with sweating, breathlessness, nausea or light-headedness) that is severe, getting worse or still there after 10 minutes of rest.
  • New chest pain that comes on with exertion and settles with rest: stop the activity and see the GP the same or next day. Call 000 if it comes on at rest or lasts more than 10 minutes.
  • Go to ED for vomiting blood or black stools; call 000 if vomiting a lot of blood or feeling faint or collapsing.
  • See the GP promptly for trouble swallowing, weight loss, repeated vomiting or tiredness.
  • Review in 4 to 8 weeks to check the PPI response and step down.
  • Follow up the gastroscopy result.
  • Arrange a diabetes and cardiovascular risk review.
points: Burning retrosternal pain after meals, worse lying down, with an acid taste and a night cough, is typical of GORD, which is a clinical diagnosis.
Chest pain worse with exercise in a middle-aged man with diabetes needs an ECG and a clear exertion history. A normal resting ECG does not exclude stable angina.

GORD management starts with lifestyle changes (smaller, earlier, less spicy and fatty meals, raising the head of the bed, weight loss), then a standard-dose PPI before a meal for 4 to 8 weeks, then stepping down to the lowest effective dose.

Endoscopy is indicated for alarm features (dysphagia, weight loss, vomiting, anaemia, haematemesis or melaena), failure of a PPI trial, new-onset symptoms in an older patient (over 50 or 55 depending on the source), especially with Barrett's risk factors, an uncertain diagnosis, and Barrett's surveillance.

Barrett's oesophagus is replacement of the squamous lining of the lower oesophagus by columnar epithelium with intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells). It is not cancer but can progress through dysplasia to adenocarcinoma, so it needs endoscopic surveillance.
